newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain asserts right to be in euro "vanguard".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain asserts right to be in euro "vanguard".

text.p: Trumpeting his government's economic successes, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar declared on Thursday Spain has earned the right to join the "vanguard" of nations that will launch Europe's single currency.

Just one day after the European Commission said it expected Spain to reduce its budget deficit this year to single currency standards, Aznar said the nation would easily meet the five economic prerequisites for the euro.

"In a very short period of time, Spain has passed from not fulfilling any criteria required to be part of the countries launching Europe's single currency to where it can form part of the vanguard," Aznar told reporters.

The EU Commission forecast that Aznar's conservative minority government would manage to narrow the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, the single currency reference value, from 4.4 percent in 1996 and 6.6 percent in 1995.
"That was clear backing to the Spanish economy and to the economy policy the government is developing," Aznar said, speaking in the garden of the prime minister's residence.
"And it also underscores the credibility and the stability of the Spanish economy," he told reporters.

The Popular Party, which took over the government last spring after 13 years of Socialist rule, has made joining Europe's Economic and Monetary Union at launch in 1999 the cornerstone of its European policy.

It has already managed to fulfil three of the five criteria, having brought inflation down sharply, helped stabilise the notoriously wobbly peseta, and fostered a dramatic decline in long-term interest rates.

In addition to narrowing the deficit, the government has pledged to bring down its debt burden, part of the single currency requirement, although the debt level itself will not fall to the 60 percent single currency reference value.
"We have passed from not fulfilling any criteria one year ago to meeting three out of five," Aznar said.
"I am convinced at the end of this year Spain will meet comfortably and with rigour and security these targets, and that we'll be part of the leading countries," he said.
The decision on who will join in and who will be shut out of the euro's debut will be made in the spring of 1998 based on the 1997 performance of the five economic criteria.
While convinced it will make the cut next spring, Spain is acutely conscious that its short history of economic stability causes great unease among some of its European brethren.

Early this year, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the track record to join the euro launch. Although he named no names, market participants believed he was targeting Italy, Spain and Portugal, which have been dubbed the "Club Med" countries.

While the EU Commission's relatively upbeat report made no firm statement on which countries will join the euro's first wave, Aznar was clearly elated with the recognition given to Spain's economic accomplishments.
"We have a very optimistic picture, backed by international bodies. And for the first time they are telling us that we have every possibility to enter, that we can enter," Aznar said.
